speaker: SPEAKER_01
transcript: . Welcome to On The Way. This is Tony Chris, and this is Podcast number 22. Today I want to talk to you about the ancient trade routes. You see, it's very important that we understand the geography and the historical context of the Bible in order to understand it. God by design chose the land of Israel. What is called the land of Israel today, ancient Canaan, and all of that fertile crescent and Mesopotamia Valley on purpose. God does nothing by accident. It really is the cradle of civilization, and it is where everything began, and it is where everything will end. I personally believe that Mount Moriah, Mount Moriah, in Jerusalem is the place where God created Adam. I believe it's where it all began, but that's for another podcast. But I do want to tell you about the strategic importance of the land bridge, the land in between called the land of Israel today. You see, it is the land bridge between Asia to the north, Europe to the west, and Africa to the south. That is where it all began, and that's where it all will end up. And there were three main trade routes that went north to south that connected Asia to the north and to the east, and then west through what is modern day Turkey, across the Hellespont, across the Dardenaels, across the Bosterers, into the area we call Western Europe today, or Greece, and then Macedonia, and so forth. That is Western Europe. And so these trade routes ran in ancient times all through Israel. And there were three main routes and then some subroutes. I want to talk to you about the main route of the sea. It was called in Latin the Viamaris, the Way of the Sea. And it ran from Egypt where the Suez Canal is today, all the way up to the Jezreel Valley, and then from there it would split east or it would split to the west and north. And so this Viamaris ran through what is modern day gods of today down near Egypt. And if you recall, this area was mentioned in the Exodus when God says, "I'm not going to take you the way of the sea, the Viamaris, but I'm going to take you through the desert because the Egyptians had fortresses and military stations throughout that Viamaris and God said, "I don't want to take the people that way because if I take the people that way they will see war and want to turn back." And so he took them the way of the Sinai Peninsula. And so the Viamaris is an ancient trade route and it was used from time immemorial. And so you came north from Egypt and you would come through what is the Gaza Strip today. You would come up the coastal plain and there were stations along the way where there were springs where cities would spring up and where there would be outposts and you would make your way until you came to a series of mountains which we call the Carmel Mountain Range which is the finger mountain in the very north into the west from the Samaritan Mountains which run from the Jezreel Valley all the way down to Jerusalem and past. So those north of Jerusalem are called the Samaritan Mountains and below that they are called the Judean Mountains or the Judean Hills. And so I'm giving you the geography of the land because it's very important that we understand it because much of biblical history and battles and so forth happened on these trade routes and that's also where the cities came into existence. So when you came to the Carmel Mountain Range you could not overcome it you couldn't climb it. It was like a blast and the seed blocked you on the west and so there were passes along the way. The primary pass was the one that came out into the Jezreel Valley from the south. It would come out at an ancient city called Megiddo. Now Megiddo is where we get the word Megeden. Armageddon or Armageddon means the mountain of Megiddo and that Jezreel Valley is called the Valley of Armageddon because it is overlooked by this ancient city called Megiddo. Now Megiddo like all ancient cities had to have certain things to be a city. First of all it had to have a water source. It had to have water to live in a desert land just like anywhere else in the world but especially in a land that is a southern California climate in the United States. And so they had to have water. They were usually located the cities near a trade route and this was the primary trade route that emptied out into the Jezreel Valley from the south and from the north as you came from the Galilean Mountains from the north. And you had this huge valley that was miles in diameter and crisscrossed. And so this is where Megiddo was built. It was one of the chariot cities of Solomon which overlooked this valley, the central valley, the valley of Jezreel. In the north you had another chariot city called Hotsor, H-A-Z-O-R in our English versions. And then to the south looking over the Agilon or Aiolon Valley was the city of Gazer, G-E-Z-E-R. And so those were Solomon's three chariot cities that overlooked these great gateways on the V.M.R.S. And so when you come to the Jezreel Valley, you come out at Megiddo. And Megiddo had springs, it had great access to the V.M.R.S. overlooking the valley. But it also had fertile fields around it which you had to have grain. You had to have food and vegetables. And so all of the things around Megiddo were exactly what was needed for a great city. In our next podcast we will talk about the nature of these ancient cities. But for right now it's enough for us to know that the V.M.R.S. was the main trade route north and south for the people of ancient times in the Middle East. We're on the way. This is Tony Chris

explicit_propositions.text: The land of Israel, known historically as ancient Canaan, lies within the fertile crescent and Mesopotamia Valley.
The land of Israel functions as a geographic land bridge connecting Asia, Europe, and Africa.
Three major trade routes existed in antiquity running north-south through ancient Israel.
Megiddo is located at a key pass through the Carmel Mountain Range and overlooks the Jezreel Valley.
God intentionally chose the land of Israel as a location for human history and divine events.
The Viamaris, or Way of the Sea, was the primary maritime trade route extending from Egypt through modern-day Gaza to the Jezreel Valley.
During the Exodus, God avoided leading the Israelites via the Viamaris due to fear of warfare causing them to retreat.
Mount Moriah in Jerusalem is believed by the speaker to be the site where God created Adam.
Armageddon derives its name from the ancient city of Megiddo and refers to the Valley of Armageddon.
Solomon established three chariot cities—Megiddo, Hazor, and Gezer—along the Viamaris to control trade and defense.

assumptions.text: Divine intentionality underlies geographical features and historical developments in the region.
Biblical narratives contain literal historical truths that inform geographic and political understanding.
Geographic centrality equates to theological significance in the divine plan.
Cities in arid regions required proximity to both water sources and trade routes to survive and thrive.
Ancient trade routes were critical determinants of urban development and military strategy.
The speaker’s interpretation of scripture carries authoritative weight for understanding history and geography.
The term 'cradle of civilization' implies a unique moral and spiritual origin point for humanity.
Military threats along trade routes necessitate strategic avoidance in religiously guided journeys.
Topographical barriers like mountain ranges naturally create choke points that become centers of conflict and settlement.
Future podcasts will build upon current claims without contradiction, maintaining coherence in narrative progression.
